title: Ideals of a valuation ring and ideals of its value group
statement: Let $K$ be a field [def-weil-field] and $A\subseteq K$ a valuation ring, meaning that for every $a\in K^\times$ at least one of $a,a^{-1}$ lies in $A$. Let $\Gamma=K^\times/A^\times$ with its ordered-abelian-group structure given by $[x]\le [y]$ iff $y/x\in A$. Call an ideal of $\Gamma$ a subset $I\subseteq\Gamma_{\ge0}$ that is upward closed, and call it prime if $0\notin I$ and $\gamma+\delta\in I$ for nonnegative $\gamma,\delta$ implies $\gamma\in I$ or $\delta\in I$. Then the ideals of $A$, ordered by inclusion, are canonically in an inclusion-preserving bijection with the ideals of $\Gamma$, and prime ideals correspond to prime ideals.

source.place: Tag 00IH, lemma-ideals-valuation-ring (the value-group ideal correspondence and preservation of prime ideals).

proof.text: For an ideal J of A define V(J) = {[a] in Gamma : a is nonzero and a is in J}. This is well defined on classes because multiplying a by a unit of A preserves membership in J. Every class in Gamma_{>=0} has a representative in A, since [1] <= [x] means x is in A. If [a] is in V(J) and [a] <= [b], then b/a is in A, hence b = a(b/a) is in J; therefore V(J) is an upward-closed subset of Gamma_{>=0}.

source.place: Tag 00IE value-group definition and Tag 00IH, proof of lemma-ideals-valuation-ring (the value-set construction).

proof.text: Conversely, for an ideal I of Gamma define R(I) = {0} union {a in A nonzero : [a] is in I}. It is an ideal of A. It is closed under multiplication by A by upward closure. For addition, if a,b are nonzero elements of R(I), the valuation class of a+b (when a+b is nonzero) is at least the smaller of [a] and [b]: after interchanging, b/a is in A, so a+b = a(1+b/a) and 1+b/a is in A. Since I is upward closed, [a+b] belongs to I; the case a+b=0 is immediate. Thus R(I) is an ideal.

source.place: Tag 00IE value-group order and Tag 00IH, proof of lemma-ideals-valuation-ring (construction from an upward-closed value set).

proof.text: The two constructions are inverse. For an ideal J, an element a is nonzero and belongs to R(V(J)) exactly when its class belongs to V(J), which by definition is exactly a in J; adjoining zero gives R(V(J)) = J. For an ideal I, every gamma in I has a representative a in A because gamma is nonnegative, and then [a] belongs to I, so gamma belongs to V(R(I)); the reverse inclusion is the defining condition. Hence V and R give a canonical bijection, and both constructions plainly preserve inclusion.

source.place: Tag 00IH, lemma-ideals-valuation-ring (inverse constructions and inclusion preservation).

proof.text: The bijection preserves primality. If J is a proper prime ideal of A, then 0 is not in V(J), since a nonnegative class 0 has a unit representative and J contains no unit. If gamma+delta is in V(J), choose representatives a,b in A with classes gamma,delta; then ab is in J, so a or b is in J, and gamma or delta is in V(J). Conversely, if I is prime and ab is in R(I) for a,b in A, then either ab=0 (forcing a=0 or b=0 because A is a domain) or [a]+[b]=[ab] lies in I; primality gives [a] or [b] in I, hence a or b in R(I). Also 0 is not in I precisely when R(I) is proper: if 0 were in I, upward closure would put every nonnegative class in I, including the class of 1, and R(I)=A; if R(I)=A then 1 is in R(I), so 0 is in I. Therefore prime ideals correspond in both directions.
